source_refs.note: Topic 27.1.1 (PDF 163-164). The insulin note and the link to glycogen stores for muscular activity follow the learning outcomes.

blocks.text: Carbohydrates have a complex role in human health. They are essential for energy and nutrients, but the type and amount eaten have a major effect on health; choosing the right carbohydrates and a balanced intake reduces the risk of disease.

items: Simple sugars such as glucose are the main source of energy for cells: they are easily absorbed and metabolised, 1 g of glucose providing about 15.6 kJ. Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles, which is why animals and humans keep glycogen stores for sustained muscular activity.

Normal blood glucose is about 70-110 mg/dL, varying slightly during the day, and is controlled by the hormones insulin and glucagon. If blood glucose rises above the normal range it can lead to diabetes, a chronic condition in which the pancreas does not produce enough insulin or the body cannot use it effectively. Uncontrolled diabetes causes hyperglycaemia (high blood sugar), which over time can damage nerves and blood vessels. Too little carbohydrate can cause fatigue and reduced physical and mental performance.

Fructose provides energy during metabolism, but a high intake causes obesity (excess body fat). Diets high in refined sugars are linked with a higher risk of chronic diseases such as diabetes, heart disease and some cancers, while complex carbohydrates and fibre protect health.
When the body has enough carbohydrate for its energy needs it uses it, instead of breaking down proteins or fats for fuel.

blocks.title: Insulin
blocks.text: Insulin is a protein hormone made by the pancreas. Its deficiency, or the body's failure to use it, leads to diabetes mellitus (topic 27.2.2).

blocks.prompt: What happens to excess glucose in the body, and which hormones control blood glucose?
blocks.explanation: It is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles; insulin and glucagon control the blood glucose level.

items: Glucose: main cell fuel (about 15.6 kJ per g); excess stored as glycogen.
Blood glucose 70-110 mg/dL, controlled by insulin and glucagon; too high: diabetes.
Refined sugars raise disease risk; complex carbohydrates and fibre protect.
